prerequisites: Introductory notions of processors, memory, and I/O devices
Organization of a process memory (global data area, stack, and heap)

learning_outcomes.text: At the end of the course, students know and understand: the fundamentals of Boolean algebra; the operation of logic gates; the criteria for the synthesis of combinational and sequential networks; the instruction execution model; the main components of a processor; computer arithmetic; the memory hierarchy; the role of mass storage devices and peripherals.

Students are able to apply the knowledge acquired to design simple combinational networks and finite-state machines, interpret the behaviour of a processor, write and analyse simple RISC-V assembly programs, and evaluate the effects of architectural choices on performance.

Students are able to critically evaluate alternative design solutions at the logical and architectural levels, interpret performance measures and indicators, and recognise the trade-offs among cost, complexity, capacity, and speed.

Students are able to describe the organization of a computer using appropriate technical language, justify the choices made in the synthesis of simple circuits, and illustrate the operation of instructions and architectural components.

Students develop the ability to independently explore topics in computer architecture, consult technical documentation and reference manuals, and connect the course contents with subsequent courses in the computer science and engineering area.

syllabus_topics: Boolean algebra and representation of logic functions
Logic gates and basic digital circuits
Analysis and synthesis of combinational machines
Computers: abstractions, technology, and levels of organization
Instructions and the language of computers
Structure and operation of the processor
Memory hierarchy, cache, and main memory
Mass storage devices and other peripherals
Elements of RISC-V assembly programming and the relationship among instructions, processor, and memory
assessment_rules: The final examination consists of a RISC-V assembly programming test followed by an oral examination. Admission to the oral examination is allowed only after passing the assembly test, for which no numerical grade is assigned. The final grade is expressed out of 30. Assessment criteria include relevance and correctness of answers, quality of reasoning, ability to apply methods, proper use of technical language, and ability to connect logical, architectural, and performance-related aspects.
bibliography: D. A. Patterson, J. L. Hennessy, Struttura e progetto dei calcolatori. Progettare con RISC-V, 2nd edition, Zanichelli, 2023.
degree: Laurea in Ingegneria Informatica (Computer Engineering), classe L-8 Classe delle lauree in Ingegneria dell'informazione
